mem-back-mechanic-ch15-rule6-content.content: Chapter 15 of 'The Back Mechanic' by Stuart McGill covers Rule #6, 'Crawl Before You Walk, Walk Before You Run': progressive movement retraining is essential for permanent back-pain relief, and each level should be mastered before advancing. Key teachings: (1) 'Be still to heal' (Rule #2) becomes a daily-life habit of moving with a relatively still lumbar spine; (2) progression sequence: neutral-spine marching in place (the 'crawl' stage) then walking with neutral spine (stand tall, use the core to lock the neutral spine, swing arms from the shoulders opposite to the legs, take sitting breaks when pain approaches) then hip-hinge (axis of movement at the hips, not the low back; lumbar spine stays neutral and protected) then full-body rotation (chest, navel, and hips move together via hips, knees, and pelvis; rib cage stays locked to the pelvis) then torso rotation combining hip-hinge and squat for everyday tasks like unloading a dishwasher; (3) troubleshooting: if any movement hurts, regress to the last pain-free step (e.g., marching in place) for a few days before progressing again; knee pain means pivot the feet or drop into a catcher-style squat; back pain likely means twisting at the waist, rounding the back, or insufficient glute strength. The user sent this full chapter text on 2023-05-20 and explicitly asked to keep it in memory as source material.

appliedEdits.title: Ear tube surgery decision study design for child's recurrent ear infections (May 2023)
appliedEdits.content: On 2023-05-24 the user asked to design a study that would help a parent decide among courses of action for a child's recurrent ear infections: getting ear tube surgery, waiting a few more months to see if infection frequency goes down, refusing antibiotics to see if the body fights off the infection on its own, or continuing antibiotics as infections come. The working design developed across the session is a four-arm randomized controlled trial (ear tube surgery; wait-and-see; refusing antibiotics; antibiotics as infections occur) with the hypothesis that ear tube surgery reduces the frequency of ear infections compared with the other options. Design elements established with the user: the wait-and-see group serves as the control; the independent variable is the type of treatment and the dependent variable is the frequency of ear infections; sample size is not yet fixed and depends on desired precision, statistical power, and outcome variability; data would be quantified as number of ear infections per child per year and infection duration, analyzed with t-tests, ANOVA, or chi-squared tests. The user is progressively working through research methodology concepts (hypothesis, control group, variables, sample size, quantification), consistent with a study-design exercise; it is not established whether the decision is personal to the user's family.
appliedEdits.reason: Six user turns establish an ongoing study-design project with no existing harness coverage; recording the design state (arms, hypothesis, control, variables, quantification approach) lets future sessions continue or refine the study without re-deriving it.

appliedEdits.content: On 2023-05-24 the user shared a passage about Dr. Scott Nema, who has studied Antarctic worms (nematodes) in the McMurdo Dry Valleys for the past 25 austral summers, collecting data on their abundance, spatial distribution, survival strategies, and trophic habits. According to the passage, colleagues' careful temperature measurements show soil temperatures became significantly cooler between 1986 and 2000 (Fig. 4.1) while nematode abundance decreased significantly over the same period (Fig. 4.2), and Dr. Nema suspects that in response to climate change the rate and amount of carbon cycled in Antarctic soil ecosystems will decrease significantly. The passage was summarized, but the user asked no follow-up question, so the purpose (e.g., coursework reading or data-interpretation exercise) is unconfirmed.
